The Music Room

Everything in this room is old, real, and free. These are complete recordings — nothing trimmed, nothing looped — kept here with the names of the people who made and shared them, because a gift should carry its giver’s name. Every piece on the shelf carries its brief history with it — what is documented, and no more.

Press play, and read with music in the room. One practical word: open this page in its own tab, and the music will keep playing while you read elsewhere in the library.

Songs: The Epitaph of Seikilos · Veni Sancte Spiritus · Rorate Caeli · Gloria · Samaii Hijaz Kar Kurdi · Taxim Hicaz · Otar Amayi Champeqi Vra · O Frondens Virga · Apolytikion of Pentecost · Martyrs’ Prayer — Monday Matins · Sermon of Sadness · Mokats Mirza · Alagyaz – Xnki tsar · The Four Shofar Calls · Song of Songs, Chapter 1 · O Heavenly King — Znamenny Chant · Omar Rabbi Elozor · Hayom Haras Olam · Yiru Eineinu · Kevakores Rohe Edro

Bells of the World: The Bells of Mülheim · The Bells of St. Jodok · The Bells of St. Matthias · The Bells of Omsk · The Bells of Kirkbymoorside · The Bells of St. Gallen · The Bells of Fribourg · The Bells of St. Albani · The Bells of St. Clement Danes · The Bells of Clelles

The Oldest Song in the World

The Epitaph of Seikilos

The oldest complete song in the world that survives with its music — a Greek song carved on a tombstone near Tralles some nineteen centuries ago, set there, its inscription says, as “a long-lasting sign of deathless remembrance.” The stone preserves the words and the melody together, so the song reaches us whole — nothing reconstructed, nothing guessed. It is sung here in its own Koine Greek.

Sung and uploaded by Marcus Harvey · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 — shared here under the same license.

Veni Sancte Spiritus

The great sequence of Pentecost — “Come, Holy Spirit” — the medieval Church’s long liturgical poem for the feast, sung in the Mass before the Gospel. Sequences were once sung by the hundred across Europe; this is one of the few the Church kept in her Mass, and it has been sung at Pentecost ever since. It is sung here in Gregorian chant by a single voice, Membeth.

Recorded by Membeth · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

Rorate Caeli

The introit of Advent: “Drop down, ye heavens, from above, and let the skies pour down righteousness” — Isaiah’s words (45:8) set as the opening chant of the Advent Mass, the Church’s cry for the coming of Christ at the dark turning of the year. Its first two words named whole services — the Rorate Masses, sung by candlelight before dawn through Advent. It is sung here in Gregorian chant.

Recorded by Inritter · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 — shared here under the same license.

Gloria

“Glory to God in the highest” — the Gloria, the angels’ song over Bethlehem (Luke 2:14) grown into the Church’s great hymn of the Mass, sung on Sundays and feasts outside the penitential seasons. This is Gloria no. 5, as the Roman Gradual — the Church’s own chant book — numbers its settings of the hymn, sung solo in Gregorian chant.

Sung by CyclePat · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0

Samaii Hijaz Kar Kurdi

A sama‘i — a measured instrumental form of the Arab and Ottoman classical tradition, built of contrasting sections around a returning refrain — in the Hijaz Kar Kurd mode, played on the oud by the Lebanese musician Chahadé Saadé. The recording is an Odeon 78 rpm pressing from about 1926 (record no. X35285), and the gentle surface sound of shellac rides in its voice — the sound of music’s first recording age in the Levant.

Played by Chahadé Saadé · Odeon record no. X35285 · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

Taxim Hicaz

A taxim is a solo improvisation — a musician thinking aloud inside a mode, testing its paths before the company joins — here in the Hicaz mode, played by Ahmed Djewdet and recorded in Turkey in 1928 for a Polydor 78 (record no. V 43163). The record never names his instrument, so neither do we: what the disc documented is the man, the mode, and the music, and this card keeps exactly that faith.

Played by Ahmed Djewdet · Polydor record no. V 43163 · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

Otar Amayi Champeqi Vra

The duduk is Armenia’s ancient double-reed instrument, its body traditionally carved from apricot wood, with a voice nearer the human throat than any other reed. Here it plays the Armenian folk song “Otar Amayi Champeqi Vra,” performed by Ikuzusotnek. The shelf claims nothing for the melody beyond what is documented — the tune, the instrument, and the hands that played it — and lets the music carry the rest.

Performed by Ikuzusotnek · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 — shared here under the same license.

O Frondens Virga

“O frondens virga” — “O leafy branch” — an antiphon of Hildegard of Bingen, the twelfth-century abbess, visionary, and composer: praise of the greening freshness of God, from her Symphonia, the cycle of songs she wrote for the liturgy of her own sisters. (The Commons page misattributes it to her Ordo Virtutum; the antiphon belongs to the Symphonia.) It is sung here in Latin by a single voice, Makemi.

Sung by Makemi · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

Apolytikion of Pentecost

The Apolytikion of Pentecost — “Blessed art Thou, O Christ our God…” — the festal hymn of Pentecost in the Byzantine rite, the chant tradition of the Greek East, where a feast’s apolytikion carries its whole theology in a few lines. It is sung here by David W. Solomons as solo cantor, in his own arrangement, and shared under the same license it rides on here.

Arranged and performed by David W. Solomons · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 — shared here under the same license.

Martyrs’ Prayer — Monday Matins

A martyrs’ prayer for Monday Matins in the Chaldean rite — the Syriac-speaking tradition of the Church of the East — attributed to Maruthas of Martyropolis. It is chanted here by the Ritual Ensemble of the Chaldean Church of the East in Jönköping, Sweden: an ancient Mesopotamian liturgy carried, as so often in its long history, by a church far from home.

Chanted by the Ritual Ensemble of the Chaldean Church of the East, Jönköping · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0

Sermon of Sadness

“Karozutha d’Hasha” — the “Proclamation of Sadness” — a Syriac sacred hymn, sung here by Hanna Petros, composer and cantor of the Assyrian Church of the East, in his own voice on an early recording. Commons keeps four tracks of this one hymn from him, parts or takes of a single work; the third track hangs here.

Sung by Hanna Petros · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

Mokats Mirza

Komitas — Soghomon Soghomonian (1869–1935) — the priest and composer who founded Armenian music by walking the villages and writing down thousands of folk songs before they could vanish. “Mokats Mirza” is one of those songs, a folk song and not a liturgy, shelved as what it is: a voice-treasure. Here the collector sings it himself, on one of the early recordings that preserve his own voice. The Commons page does not date the track; it belongs to the same early-recording world as the dated 1912 disc beside it.

Sung by Komitas · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

Alagyaz – Xnki tsar

“Alagyaz – Xnki tsar” — “Incense Tree” — an Armenian folk song in Komitas’s own arrangement, recorded in 1912: Armenak Shahmuradyan (1878–1939), tenor, singing, and Komitas himself accompanying at the piano. A shellac disc from the last years of the old world, carrying two of the great carriers of Armenia’s song in a single groove.

Armenak Shahmuradyan, tenor · Komitas at the piano · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

The Trumpet of Scripture

The Four Shofar Calls

Not a song but a voice: the shofar, the ram’s horn of Scripture — sounded at Sinai, around Jericho’s walls, and through the Psalms — blown by Tom A. Fürstenberg, chazzan and ba’al tokea (master of the blowing) of the Beth Shoshanna community in Deventer, the Netherlands. You hear the four traditional calls in their order: Tekiah, the single blast; Shevarim, three wailing notes; Teruah, the short cries; and Tekiah Gedolah, the great long blast that closes the set. The recording is complete at thirty-three seconds.

Blown by Tom A. Fürstenberg · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 — shared here under the same license.

Song of Songs, Chapter 1

Scripture sung, not read: the first chapter of Shir Hashirim — the Song of Songs — chanted according to the Sephardic-Jerusalem tradition, the cantillation of Jerusalem’s Sephardic community. This is chapter 1 of 8: the same voice has sung all eight chapters, and all eight stand on Commons under the same license; the first chapter hangs here, and the rest are named in Sources.

Chanted by A0~commonswiki · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 — shared here under the same license.

O Heavenly King — Znamenny Chant

“O Heavenly King” — Tsaryu Nebesny — sung in Znamenny chant, the unison, melismatic liturgical singing of the Russian Orthodox Church, named for the znamëna (“banners”), the hook-shaped signs of its stolp notation, and ordered in eight tones. It is sung here by a male chamber choir of the Moscow Patriarchate.

Moscow Patriarchal Choir · Wikimedia Commons · CC0 — given to the public domain

An Edison Diamond Disc, 1919

Omar Rabbi Elozor

Cantor Meyer Kanewsky and his choir, recorded for Edison Records on 18 January 1919 — among the earliest cantorial recordings ever made. Honestly shelved: the text is not Scripture but the closing passage of the Talmud’s Tractate Berakhot, sung in the Friday night and Sabbath morning services — “Said Rabbi Elazar, quoting Rabbi Chaninah: Scholars increase the levels of peace in the world.” It hangs here as what it is: a voice-treasure from the world that guarded the text, labeled as itself.

Cantor Meyer Kanewsky and choir · Edison Diamond Disc 75001-R, 1919 · Source: Library of Congress · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

Warsaw, 1908

Hayom Haras Olam

“Today is the birthday of the world” — the opening of the Rosh Hashanah prayer Hayom Harat Olam, sung by Gershon Sirota (1874–1943) with the Warsaw Synagogue Choir, recorded in Warsaw in 1908 — the year Sirota became head cantor of the Tłomackie Street Synagogue. These Warsaw discs are among the earliest recordings of Jewish liturgical chant ever made.

Gershon Sirota with the Warsaw Synagogue Choir · Gramophone, Warsaw, 1908 · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

Warsaw, 1909

Yiru Eineinu

“May our eyes behold Your return to Zion in mercy” — the incipit of a passage from the Retzei blessing of the Amidah, the standing prayer at the center of Jewish services. Gershon Sirota sings it, recorded in Warsaw on 23 June 1909, the year after he became head cantor of the Tłomackie Street Synagogue.

Gershon Sirota · Gramophone, Warsaw, 1909 · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

Warsaw, 1908

Kevakores Rohe Edro

“As a shepherd examines his flock” — the great shepherd passage of Unetanneh Tokef, the central prayer of the Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur Musaf services. Gershon Sirota sings it in the same 1908 Warsaw session as the Hayom Haras Olam beside it on this shelf — this disc’s matrix number follows that one’s in sequence. It is a complete single side of a 78, exactly as issued.

Gershon Sirota · Gramophone, Warsaw, 1908 · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

Bells of the World

And the room has bells. Ten towers whose bells were given to the world freely — each kept with the church it hangs in, the face of its tower, and a little of its story.

Evangelische Kirche · Mülheim an der Mosel, Germany

The Bells of Mülheim

The Protestant church of Mülheim, a wine village on the Moselle in Rhineland-Palatinate, is a baroque church built in 1669–1675 around an older Romanesque tower, in one of the oldest Protestant parishes of the Rhineland. You hear its second and third bells. And these are this site’s own Sabbath bells: the first three strikes of this very recording are the peal that rings the weekly teaching in — its ringer, Helge Klaus Rieder, also took the photograph.

Bells recorded by Helge Klaus Rieder · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0
Photograph by Helge Klaus Rieder · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 — shared here under the same license.

Pfarrkirche St. Jodok · Schruns, Austria

The Bells of St. Jodok

The parish church of St. Jodok — the Schrunser Münster — stands in the centre of Schruns, a market town in Austria’s Montafon valley, 690 metres up in the Vorarlberg Alps. A chapel of St. Jodok here is first named in a register of 1433, and the church is still the town’s heart, a protected monument. Its bells ring out over the town, recorded by Helge Klaus Rieder and given to everyone, freely, under CC0.

Bells recorded by Helge Klaus Rieder · Wikimedia Commons · CC0 — given to the public domain
Photograph by Schlaier · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 — shared here under the same license.

Benediktinerabtei St. Matthias · Trier, Germany

The Bells of St. Matthias

The abbey church of St. Matthias in Trier is the Romanesque basilica of a Benedictine abbey whose monks have lived on this ground since late antiquity. Since the twelfth century it has guarded the tomb of the Apostle Matthias — the only apostle’s grave in Germany, and north of the Alps — and pilgrims still seek it out. Here its bells ring on for three and a half minutes, recorded by Helge Klaus Rieder and given freely under CC0.

Bells recorded by Helge Klaus Rieder · Wikimedia Commons · CC0 — given to the public domain
Photograph by Berthold Werner · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

St. Nicholas Cossack Cathedral · Omsk, Russia

The Bells of Omsk

St. Nicholas Cossack Cathedral in Omsk, Siberia, was raised in the 1840s as the cathedral of the Siberian Cossack Host, and stands among the oldest churches in the city. Its bells ring here for seven minutes in the Russian zvon manner — rhythmic patterns sounded across the whole belfry together, the voice that marked feasts and hours across old Russia. Zabuhailo recorded them and gave the recording to everyone, freely, under CC0.

Bells recorded by Zabuhailo · Wikimedia Commons · CC0 — given to the public domain
Photograph by Ymblanter · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0 — shared here under the same license.

All Saints Church · Kirkbymoorside, England

The Bells of Kirkbymoorside

All Saints church stands over Kirkbymoorside, a market town in North Yorkshire, and its six bells are rung in the English manner: change ringing, in which the bells swing full-circle and sound in ever-shifting mathematical orders, rung by the tower’s own ringers. The recording was made in the belfry by Helge Klaus Rieder — the same bell-hunter who recorded the three German towers on this shelf — and given freely under CC0; what you hear is the audio of his film, the picture set aside.

Bells recorded by Helge Klaus Rieder · Wikimedia Commons · CC0 — given to the public domain
Photograph by Peter Wood · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 — shared here under the same license.

Abbey Cathedral of St. Gallen · St. Gallen, Switzerland

The Bells of St. Gallen

The abbey cathedral of St. Gallen carries a peal of twelve bells, nine of them the cathedral peal proper. Its Trinity Bell, cast in 1768 and weighing about 8,100 kg, sounds the lowest bell tone in Switzerland. What you hear is the close of the full peal as it is rung on Saturdays at half past five in the evening — the deepest bell resting — recorded by Martin Thurnherr.

Bells recorded by Martin Thurnherr · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 — shared here under the same license.
Photograph by Shesmax · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 — shared here under the same license.

St. Nicholas Cathedral · Fribourg, Switzerland

The Bells of Fribourg

Fribourg’s Gothic cathedral was begun in 1283 and completed around 1430, its west tower finished in 1490. Thirteen bells hang in the west tower and the choir bell tower — among them the oldest bell still ringing in Switzerland, cast in Aarau in 1367 by Walter Reber. What you hear is the opening of the full peal that rings in Sunday on Saturday evening, recorded by Martin Thurnherr.

Bells recorded by Martin Thurnherr · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 — shared here under the same license.
Photograph by GFreihalter · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 — shared here under the same license.

St. Albani Church · Göttingen, Germany

The Bells of St. Albani

St. Albani is Göttingen’s oldest church: a church dedicated to St. Alban stood on this ground from the early eleventh century, and the present three-aisled Gothic hall church was built from 1423. Its bells sound here in full for six and a half minutes — the whole peal, given time to breathe — recorded by Ramessos and given to everyone, freely, in the public domain.

Bells recorded by Ramessos · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain
Photograph by Daniel Schwen · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.5 — shared here under the same license.

St. Clement Danes · London, England

The Bells of St. Clement Danes

Christopher Wren’s church on the Strand, completed in 1682, is the central church of the Royal Air Force — and the St. Clement’s of “Oranges and Lemons,” whose tune its bells play daily at nine, noon, three and six. Its ten bells fell and cracked in the Blitz fire of 10 May 1941 and were recast after the war. This is the nine o’clock playing, recorded by Kevin Laurence.

Bells recorded by Kevin Laurence · Wikimedia Commons · CC0 — given to the public domain
Photograph by Jim Osley · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0 — shared here under the same license.

Sainte-Marie de l’Assomption · Clelles, France

The Bells of Clelles

The church of this village in the Trièves is first named in a papal bull of 1123, and its fifteenth-century bell tower is a listed historic monument. The tower holds a classified ensemble of nine bells with a mechanical clock and carillon machine — one of only three carillons in the Isère département — designed around the “Marie” bell of 1784. Here the carillon strikes the twelve blows of noon, recorded by Jérôme Villafuela, who also took the photograph.

Bells recorded by Jérôme Villafuela · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 — shared here under the same license.
Photograph by Jérôme Villafuela · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 — shared here under the same license.

Every recording in this room is public domain or freely licensed; the licensed pieces are shared under their own licenses, named on each card. The files were converted to a web format for this shelf and are otherwise unaltered.
